content: 1. Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim is an oral medication classified as a sulfonamide, folic acid antagonist, and anti-infective agent. It is FDA-approved for treating urinary tract infections, acute otitis media, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, shigellosis, Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia, and traveler’s diarrhea caused by susceptible strains of enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli. 2. Common adverse reactions to this medication include rash, urticaria (hives), loss of appetite, nausea, and vomiting. 3. The standard adult dosage for treating urinary tract infections is one double-strength tablet or two single-strength tablets every 12 hours for 10 to 14 days. For shigellosis, the same dosage is used for 5 days. 4. In pediatric patients, the recommended dose for urinary tract infections or acute otitis media is 40 mg/kg of sulfamethoxazole and 8 mg/kg of trimethoprim per 24 hours, divided into two doses every 12 hours for 10 days. The same dosage is used for 5 days in shigellosis treatment. 5. Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim is contraindicated in children under 2 months of age, patients with known hypersensitivity to sulfonamides or trimethoprim, those with a history of drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia, and individuals with documented megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency. 6. This medication is also contraindicated in patients with severe renal insufficiency or marked hepatic damage when renal function cannot be monitored. 7. If used during pregnancy, patients should be informed of potential risks to the fetus. 8. Fatalities associated with sulfonamide administration, though rare, have occurred due to severe reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, fulminant hepatic necrosis, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, and other blood dyscrasias. 9. Sulfonamides, including sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, should be discontinued at the first appearance of skin rash or any sign of adverse reaction, as these may progress to severe conditions like Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. 10. Patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency may experience hemolysis, which is often dose-related. 11. Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim may cause hyperkalemia, particularly in patients with underlying potassium metabolism disorders, renal insufficiency, or those taking other medications that induce hyperkalemia. Serum potassium levels should be closely monitored in these patients. 12. Severe and symptomatic hyponatremia has been reported in patients receiving this medication, especially during treatment for Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. Evaluation and correction of hyponatremia are necessary to prevent life-threatening complications. 13. 14. Complete blood counts should be performed frequently during therapy. If a significant reduction in any blood cell count is observed, the medication should be discontinued. 15. Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim may interact with other drugs, including warfarin, phenytoin, methotrexate, and digoxin, potentially altering their effects. Monitoring and dose adjustments may be necessary. 16. In elderly patients taking diuretics, particularly thiazides, there is an increased risk of thrombocytopenia with purpura when co-administered with sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. 17. This medication is classified as Pregnancy Category D by the FDA. It should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. 18. In animal studies, high doses of sulfamethoxazole or trimethoprim have been associated with teratogenic effects, such as cleft palates, at doses significantly higher than those used in humans. 19. Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim should be prescribed cautiously in patients with impaired renal or hepatic function, folate deficiency, severe allergies, or bronchial asthma. 20. Adverse effects reported during clinical trials include gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, vomiting, anorexia) and allergic skin reactions (rash, urticaria). Rare but severe reactions include Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and fulminant hepatic necrosis. 21. Post-marketing reports have identified additional adverse reactions, such as QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. These reactions are rare and typically reported voluntarily. 22. 23. Patients with AIDS may experience a higher incidence of side effects, such as rash, fever, and leukopenia, when treated with sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim for Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia compared to non-AIDS patients. 24. Co-administration of sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim with leucovorin for Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia in HIV-positive patients has been associated with treatment failure and increased mortality. This combination should be avoided. 25. Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim should not be used for treating Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections, as it does not eradicate the bacteria and may not prevent sequelae such as rheumatic fever.
